Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
The cofactors are \(A_{11} = 4\), \(A_{12} = -3\), \(A_{21} = -2\), \(A_{22} = 1\).
The cofactor matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is its transpose.
Hence \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Compute the cofactors.
\(A_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 3\), \(A_{12} = -\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -(2 + 10) = -12\), \(A_{13} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0 + 6 = 6\).
\(A_{21} = -\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = -(-1) = 1\), \(A_{22} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1 + 4 = 5\), \(A_{23} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -(0 - 2) = 2\).
\(A_{31} = \begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = -5 - 6 = -11\), \(A_{32} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = -(5 - 4) = -1\), \(A_{33} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 3 + 2 = 5\).
The cofactor matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -12 & 6 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 \\ -11 & -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(\operatorname{adj} A\) is its transpose: \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & -11 \\ -12 & 5 & -1 \\ 6 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -4 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = (2)(-6) - (3)(-4) = -12 + 12 = 0\).
For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & -3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -4 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -6 & -3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -12 + 12 & -6 + 6 \\ 24 - 24 & 12 - 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
\((\operatorname{adj} A) A = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & -3 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -4 & -6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -12 + 12 & -18 + 18 \\ 8 - 8 & 12 - 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
Also \(|A| I = 0 \cdot I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence \(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = (\operatorname{adj} A) A = |A| I\), verified.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 1(0 - 0) - (-1)(9 + 2) + 2(0 - 0) = 11\), so \(|A| I = 11 I\).
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -11 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 8 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is its transpose: \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & 2 \\ -11 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 & 2 \\ -11 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 11 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 11 \end{bmatrix} = 11 I\).
Similarly \((\operatorname{adj} A) A = 11 I\).
Hence \(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = (\operatorname{adj} A) A = |A| I\), verified.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \(A\) is upper triangular, \(|A| = 1 \times 2 \times 5 = 10 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 \\ -10 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 & 2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = \frac{1}{10}\begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 & 2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 5 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \(A\) is lower triangular, \(|A| = 1 \times 3 \times (-1) = -3 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ -9 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ -9 & -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 & 0 \\ -7 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 2(-1 - 0) - 1(4 - 0) + 3(8 - 7) = -2 - 4 + 3 = -3 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -4 & 1 \\ 5 & 23 & -11 \\ 3 & 12 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 & 3 \\ -4 & 23 & 12 \\ 1 & -11 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = -\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 & 3 \\ -4 & 23 & 12 \\ 1 & -11 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 1(8 - 6) - (-1)(0 + 9) + 2(0 - 6) = 2 + 9 - 12 = -1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -9 & -6 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -9 & -2 & 3 \\ -6 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = -\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ -9 & -2 & 3 \\ -6 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & -3 \\ 6 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ 0 & \sin\alpha & -\cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 1\big((\cos\alpha)(-\cos\alpha) - (\sin\alpha)(\sin\alpha)\big) = -(\cos^{2}\alpha + \sin^{2}\alpha) = -1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ 0 & -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ 0 & -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A = -\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha \\ 0 & -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ 0 & \sin\alpha & -\cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\).
Thus \(A^{-1} = A\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 8 \\ 7 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 18 + 49 & 24 + 63 \\ 12 + 35 & 16 + 45 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 67 & 87 \\ 47 & 61 \end{bmatrix}\), with \(|AB| = (67)(61) - (87)(47) = 4087 - 4089 = -2\).
So \((AB)^{-1} = \frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix} 61 & -87 \\ -47 & 67 \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 61 & -87 \\ -47 & 67 \end{bmatrix}\).
Now \(|A| = 15 - 14 = 1\), so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -7 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\); and \(|B| = 54 - 56 = -2\), so \(B^{-1} = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 9 & -8 \\ -7 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(B^{-1} A^{-1} = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 9 & -8 \\ -7 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -7 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = -\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 61 & -87 \\ -47 & 67 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}\), the result is verified.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} - 5A + 7I = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = O\).
From \(A^{2} - 5A + 7I = O\), we get \(7I = 5A - A^{2} = A(5I - A)\), so \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}(5I - A)\).
\(5I - A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 8 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} + aA + bI = \begin{bmatrix} 11 + 3a + b & 8 + 2a \\ 4 + a & 3 + a + b \end{bmatrix} = O\).
Equating entries: \(8 + 2a = 0 \Rightarrow a = -4\), which also satisfies \(4 + a = 0\).
Then \(11 + 3a + b = 0 \Rightarrow 11 - 12 + b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 1\), consistent with \(3 + a + b = 3 - 4 + 1 = 0\).
Hence \(a = -4\) and \(b = 1\).

We use \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}\), with \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 1 \\ -15 & 6 & -5 \\ 5 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
First find \(B^{-1}\). \(|B| = 1(3 - 0) - 2(-1 - 0) + (-2)(2 - 0) = 3 + 2 - 4 = 1\).
The cofactors give the cofactor matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 6 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(\operatorname{adj} B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
\((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 1 \\ -15 & 6 & -5 \\ 5 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 1(15 - 1) - 2(10 - 1) + 1(2 - 3) = 14 - 18 - 1 = -5\).
Using the property \(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = |A| I\), we have \(\operatorname{adj} A = |A| A^{-1}\), so \((\operatorname{adj} A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|} A = -\frac{1}{5} A\).
Also \(\operatorname{adj}(A^{-1}) = |A^{-1}|\,(A^{-1})^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\,A = -\frac{1}{5} A\) (since \(|A^{-1}| = \frac{1}{|A|}\) and \((A^{-1})^{-1} = A\)).
Both expressions equal \(-\frac{1}{5} A\), hence \([\operatorname{adj} A]^{-1} = \operatorname{adj}(A^{-1})\), verified.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), with \(|A| = -5 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.
By the definition of the inverse, \(A^{-1} A = A A^{-1} = I\).
This same relation shows that \(A\) is the inverse of \(A^{-1}\), because \(A^{-1}\) multiplied by \(A\) (on either side) yields \(I\).
Since the inverse of a matrix is unique, \((A^{-1})^{-1} = A\), verified.
